# Status

What exists, area by area, and its known limits. Each row of the two tables, with the known
limits of its area, is a file in `docs/status/` (`areas/<area>.md`, `apps/<app>.md`: the row on
the first line, the limits after it), and the rest of this page is `docs/status/page.md`.
Update them in the same change that moves an item; `lake exe lanes lint --fix` writes this page.

Proved: it lists exactly the enabled events of a state, merging states is safe, a complete PASS means every `always` property holds in every world of the instance (`Check.system_sound_of_respects`; `==` must be equality on actor states, and on the driver's state an equivalence that the driver respects, `Driver.Respects`; the hash only decides how many states are stored; `Check.system_sound` is the case where it is equality), the spec monitor accepts exactly what the spec allows, deadlines included (`Check.Monitor.ok_iff`), a monitor never holds a candidate twice (in its type), so monitors compare and hash as sets and a monitored driver respects `==` (`Service.monitored_respects`), a complete PASS of a refinement check means the monitor has a candidate in every world (`Check.refines_sound`) and the inputs, outputs and deadlines passing of every run of the instance are a trace of the spec (`Check.refines_traces`; the spec's state must have `==` as equality), and a reported violation is a real run of the semantics (`Check.system_violated`) | `Lanes/Check/`, `Lanes/Semantics/Monitor.lean`, `Lanes/Semantics/MonitorSound.lean` |
| Proof layer | `Spec`, `Refines` (weak simulation with a label map), `of_map`, `trans`, trace inclusion; system semantics as a CSLib `LTS`; `Service.spec`, over inputs and outputs (`Service In Out S T`, written before the actors), with deadlines `T` that pass as visible steps, and `System.Implements sys env svc deadlines delivered`, refinement with the system's timers that `deadlines` names firing them and the deliveries that `delivered` names passing them where a message is served (`docs/decisions/D42-a-spec-names-its-inputs-and.md`, `docs/decisions/D56-a-deadline-passes-where-it-is-served.md`; how long a deadline lasts is not modelled); every run of a system that implements a service has a sequential history of the service's acts that produces each output handed over, takes each input after it arrives and respects real-time order, a deadline passing in it exactly in the block of the position at which the run shows it (`System.Implements.history`, `System.Implements.Explains.fired`, `fires`, `System.Implements.produced`), so what is proved of the service's functions holds of the system's outputs; `Service.once`, the spec of a service whose clients name their requests, where a key takes effect at most once and an answer may be handed over again, and `System.Refines.of_handles`, the proof rule for a simulation that reads messages in flight as a set, which holds in every environment; the standard simulation of a service behind actors (`Account`: inputs pending and outputs owed on messages, in states and in a witness, the value as a relation), with which an application proves only what each step of an actor does to it (`Account.Handles`, `Account.implements`), and with deadlines what a step that passes one does (`Account.HandlesFire`, `Account.implements_timed`), each case knowing where its message came from (`System.Sent`, `System.Armed`: every message in flight is an input or one some step sends, every timer one some step arms, `System.traced`, for every system), the messages on one link in order (`linkMsgs`) with what sending, delivering the oldest, losing and a crash do to them, and refinement case by event with only the losses the environment has (`System.Refines.of_timed_events`, `of_events`; `docs/decisions/D52-standard-simulation.md`); sum lemmas. Liveness: infinite runs with stuttering (`System.Run`), weak fairness for each `Obligation` of the system on its own (deliveries, timers, starting an actor that has mail, outputs; never the environment's events), where a timer is obliged to fire only if it stays pending and no step arms it again, as in the runtime (`Obligation.Restarted`; a watchdog that is pinged forever never barks in a fair run, `examples/watchdog/Watchdog/Proofs.lean`), `System.LeadsTo` with its proof rule (`LeadsTo.ensures_of_invariant`), transitivity and monotonicity; a message in flight on a link that loses nothing, to an actor that stays up, is handed to it (`System.Run.Fair.delivered`, by what is ahead of it on its link). Fair runs exist: every finite run extends to a fair run, for every system and environment model (`System.exists_fair_run_of_run`), so every reachable state is on one. Fair runs project: a view under which each step of one system is a finite run of another and the obligations match carries fair runs to fair runs and leads-to with them (`System.View.Projects.fair_run`, `leadsTo`). A fair run of `a.join b w`, seen from `a` without the messages from outside in flight, is a fair run of `a` alone under `EnvModel.left`, state for state at corresponding positions and with the same deeds up to them (`System.Run.Fair.left`), so what `a` alone leads to of its actors it leads to in every join (`System.LeadsTo.join_left`); the same behind hidden inputs and outputs, when the output map is injective where it shows (`System.underView_projects`, `System.LeadsTo.filterMapIO`). The same of `b` under `EnvModel.right`, though `b` boots after `a`: what the boot of `a` sends `b` is from outside, so the view leaves it out and starts where `b` alone starts (`System.Run.Fair.right`, `System.LeadsTo.join_right`). What one side emits and the wiring routes to the other, which neither view shows, is handled by the other side, on a link that loses nothing, by an actor the environment does not crash and that never stops (`System.Run.Fair.routed_right`, `routed_left`, `handled_right`, `handled_left`); a receiver that is down has mail, so fairness starts it (`System.Run.Fair.handled`) | `Lanes/Semantics/` |
| Runtime | A kernel of pure functions (routing, start and stop, timers, batching, idleness) proved to follow the semantics whatever its caller does (`Kernel.exec_reachable`, `Kernel.exec_outputs`), releasing an actor that is back where a start puts it with no timers and proved to change nothing anyone can see by it (`Kernel.exec_visible`; a hundred thousand identities touched leave none in the kernel), never to lose a pending timer or spin on one (`Kernel.exec_wellFormed`), and to let neither timers nor messages starve the other (`Kernel.WellFormed.step_of_queued`, `step_of_due`), inside a shell that only performs what a pure function of each batch returns, proved to keep the journal describing the kernel, to hand an output over only after the entries that produce it are written and to save only where every output is handed over (`Batch.run_kernel`, `Batch.run_sound`): one thread per shard, bounded inbox; the actors of a wave step in parallel on Lean's task pool where the shard's own timing says it pays (`Runtime.Config.parallel := .auto`), proved to change nothing the kernel does whatever is chosen (`Kernel.runWaves_eq`, `Batch.run_spread`). A message costs the same at 1,000 and 100,000 actors, and a step updates its actor's state in place, on the shard's thread and on the pool, so on the shard's thread it costs the same whatever the state's size (`Kernel.takeState`, `Kernel.Plan.real`, `Tests/Scale.lean`). Durable with a journal: the shard replays what its kernel was asked and returns in the same state, proved for whole and torn journals and tested with SIGKILL; a journal that is damaged, another system's, or written with another codec is refused and left as it is (`Journal.open?`), and so is one whose read fails, which is not taken for a journal that is not there (`Journal.Disk.Torn.load_readings`), and one process at a time holds a journal. What the inbox decides is proved for every capacity and every sequence of operations: a take returns exactly what was taken in since the last, in order (`Mailbox.batch_since_take`), it never holds more than its capacity (`Mailbox.Reachable.bounded`), and no sleeper or waiting sender is forgotten (`Mailbox.woken_after_rest`, `Mailbox.wake_since_take`). With codecs for its actors the shard saves its kernel and cuts the journal, so a restart replays only what came after the last save: starting from a snapshot gives exactly what replaying the whole history gives (`Journal.resume_eq_recover`), and a process that dies at any point of a save, or at any byte of an append, leaves files that load as the kernel it had (`Journal.Disk.Holds.save_crash`, `append_crash`), tested by killing a process while it saves. A deploy that changes a state or message type reads the old version's files through an upgrade: they are replayed as the old version did, the kernel is migrated with a proof that every state an old actor reaches lands in an inductive invariant of the new one, and that invariant holds of every actor afterwards (`Migration.inv_exec`, `Journal.Upgrade.inv_load`); dying anywhere in the migration's writes gives the same migrated kernel (`Journal.Upgrade.begin_crash`), and the crash theorems go on from the migrated kernel (`Journal.Upgrade.holds`); `examples/migration` Several shards: `System.shard` is a system as one shard sees it, on the unchanged kernel, and `Peers` joins shards in different processes. Shards joined behave as the one system, at the level of the semantics: every state of a well-routed run, read as one state, is a state the system reaches alone up to `SysState.Equiv`, for two shards (`System.SplitReachable.merged`) and for any number (`System.shards sys hosts` with `hosts : σ.Id → Fin n`, `System.ShardsReachable.unsharded`), so its invariants hold there (`System.Invariant.split`, `split_state`, `shards`, `shards_state`); model-checked on three shards with the bank and a relay of boot actors with timers and stops | `Lanes/Runtime/`, `Lanes/Durable/`, `Lanes/Proof/Lossy.lean`, `Lanes/Durable/IO/Journal.lean` |

| Tooling | `lanes new` (its types declared with `lanes_data`), `lanes lint` (text-level, the sizes of trusted files, that every repository path a doc cites exists, and the files `--fix` writes: their line counts, the index of decisions and the numbers of new ones, the status page, the inventory), `lanes check`, `lanes inventory` (`docs/INVENTORY.md`: every public definition with its status and evidence, read from the built modules; lint fails on one of `Lanes/` without evidence that is not on `docs/inventory-none.md`); `instance_by_cases` for instances defined by cases on an identity (`Inspect` of a system whose actors differ); CI on every push to the pull request (build with warnings as errors, then lint, tests and a generated app, model checks, the differential tests against Go, the small examples, `examples/raft-kv`, `examples/ledger` and `examples/rookery` as parallel jobs, and the build and tests on macOS); the mutation gate in parallel shards, nightly, by hand and on pull requests labelled `mutants`, on GitHub's runners or a warm EC2 machine the workflow starts and stops (`docs/RUNNERS.md`); `scripts/lean-goals` for a file's errors and goals from a language server kept open; axiom gate | `LanesCli/`, `Lanes/Core/ByCases.lean`, `.github/`, `infra/`, `scripts/`, `Tests/Axioms.lean` |
| Web | HTTP/1.1 adapter whose logic is the gate, one system (`Http.gateSystem`, decisions `Gate.step`). `Http.fronted sys` is the gate joined in front of `sys` by `System.join`, and `Http.served sys` is `fronted sys` with requests its only inputs and responses its only outputs: what `Http.serve` runs (`docs/decisions/D43-one-gate.md`). Proved of `served sys` for every system, bridge and configuration: an arrival is answered at most once in any environment whose link from outside to the gate does not duplicate (`Http.served_answered_le_arrived`, `Http.kernel_served_answered_le_arrived`, with crashes, loss, reordering and duplication elsewhere allowed), a waiting request keeps its deadline armed (`Http.served_deadlines_armed`), and in every fair run in which the gate does not crash a request the gate has admitted is answered, by the system or with `504` (`Http.served_pending_leaves`, `Http.served_pending_answered`). Every request that arrives is answered, in a fair run in which the gate does not crash and the link from outside to the gate loses nothing (`Http.served_arrival_answered`, `Http.fronted_arrival_answered`, from `System.Run.Fair.delivered`: a message on a link that loses nothing to an actor that stays up is handed to it), so a request whose id is used once is answered exactly once; model-checked on two requests, with each premise shown to be needed. In `fronted sys`, outputs of `sys` that are no response and inputs that are no request pass the gate by, so a shard with peers can sit behind it (`Http.serveFronted`, `Http.serveShard`). Proved of `fronted sys` by projection from the gate alone, for every `sys`: at most once per arrival where the link from outside to the gate does not duplicate (`Http.fronted_answered_le_arrived`, from `Http.Gate.answered_le_handled`) and deadlines stay armed (`Http.fronted_deadlines_armed`); and in every fair run in which the gate does not crash a request the gate has admitted is answered (`Http.fronted_pending_leaves`, `Http.fronted_pending_answered`, from `Http.Gate.pending_leaves` and `Http.Gate.pending_answered` of the gate alone, through the hidden inputs and outputs and the join); model-checked with the properties checked of `served`, and the premises of the leads-to rule on the gate alone with the link a join gives it from outside. The theorems of `served sys` are those of `fronted sys` carried through its hidden inputs and outputs. A journal of the gate `serve` ran before `docs/decisions/D43-one-gate.md` is refused; one `serve` wrote behind a gate of other settings is replayed behind that gate and carried across (`Http.regateUpgrade`, `docs/decisions/new-journal-version.md`). The server prepares each request as its bridge says (`Bridge.prepare`, pure) on the request's own task before it enters the shard, so a password or a cookie a bridge takes out is never journalled and slow work is not done on the shard's thread (`docs/decisions/D44-request-prepared-before-journal.md`); requests and responses as data; `Html` that a model of the browser's tokenizer reads as the tree it was rendered from, text as text and attribute values as given (`Html.lex_render`), with URL attributes whose scheme, however spaced or cased, is `http`, `https`, `mailto` or `tel` (`Html.safeUrl_scheme`); scoped template macro with components, fragments and attribute splices; forms read back as written (`Http.parseForm_encodeForm`); typed routes whose links reach their route's handler (`Route.match?_link`, `Route.link_target`, `Http.dispatch_link`); htmx attributes as typed values taken from routes (`Hx.request_match?`), triggers with no script filter (`Hx.render_plain`); cookies a browser stores with exactly the attributes they name (`Http.readSetCookie_header`, `Http.setCookie_read`) and read back (`Http.parseCookies_cookieHeader`), the origin check of a form (`Http.Request.sameOrigin_iff`), a per-route body limit. Sessions and authentication: signed tokens with a purpose and form tokens bound to a session, which accept exactly what was signed (`Auth.verify_eq_some`, `Auth.checkForm_iff`) and another purpose's or session's only through an HMAC collision (`Auth.verify_sign_other`, `Auth.checkForm_other`), password digests by Argon2id compared with libsodium's `sodium_memcmp`, failed attempts that lock at their limit (`Auth.Attempts.locked_unlock_repeat`), sessions that keep the newest and close the oldest (`Auth.Sessions.ids_starts`) and end after an idle or absolute lifetime, judged at the time a request arrived, checked on use and swept on write, with no timer: an expired session is never let in again (`Auth.Sessions.accepts_iff`, `Auth.Sessions.Ended.run`). Sign-in with another service (`docs/decisions/D72-sign-in-with-oauth.md`): OAuth 2.0's authorization code flow with PKCE (S256) and OpenID Connect, decided in `Lanes/Web/Auth/OAuth.lean` and done before the system by `serve`'s `arrive` (`Lanes/Web/IO/SignIn.lean`, trusted), so no code or token is journalled; a sign-in begun is a ticket its browser keeps in a cookie under the server's tag, so beginnings take no room on the server; a callback is accepted only with its browser's ticket, for its state and its provider, before it expires (`OAuth.check_ok`), and its state is claimed once its sign-in is done, so none is accepted twice over any run (`OAuth.Used.accepted_later`, `OAuth.Used.accepted_once`), among at most `maxUsed` states kept, a full set refusing the tickets that expire no later than those it dropped (`OAuth.Used.length_claim`), model-checked against an attacker's browser that replays and swaps callbacks; an ID token is accepted only when its header names RS256 or ES256, a key of the provider's JWK Set of that algorithm and `kid` checks it, and its issuer, audience, authorized party, expiry, `nbf` within a skew and nonce pass (`OAuth.IdToken.verify_accepted`, `Jose.verify_ok`); JWK Sets are cached and fetched again at most once a minute (`OAuth.Keys.no_fetch_within`); a provider of OAuth 2.0 alone is asked its user API; the identity reaches the system in headers a client's are dropped from (`OAuth.identity?_strip`), with the provider's name for the user bounded and stripped of control characters by its type (`OAuth.DisplayName`). Signatures are checked by OpenSSL's libcrypto (`native/verify.c`, trusted) from DER written in Lean, RSA also by a Lean reference, against RFC 7515 and RFC 7520's vectors. Presets for Google and GitHub are packages under `integrations/`. The server reads and writes HTTP/1.1 itself on `Std.Net`, with no `Std.Http`: each connection is `Http.Conn.step`, pure, model-checked against a client that sends in any pieces, pipelines and leaves, and proved to write responses in the order requests were read, each once (`Http.Conn.run_writes`), to hand on only requests the strict reader reads (`Http.Conn.step_submit_read`), to keep its buffer within `message_max` and its requests in flight within `inflight_max` (`Http.Conn.run_buffer`, `run_slots`), to take nothing once closed or no longer reading (`Http.Conn.step_closed`, `step_notReading`, `step_reading`), to stop reading at a deadline (`Http.Conn.step_tick`) and to write what the client's reader reads back (`Http.Conn.read_encode`), with `100 Continue`, keep-alive, pipelining, deadlines for a slow head or body and a bound on connections (`docs/decisions/D57-the-server-runs-its-own-connections.md`). Requests may stream (the decision "Bodies and responses stream through the gate"): a body in pieces of at most `piece_max` bytes and a response in parts, Server-Sent Events among them, each piece and each pull a request of its own through the gate, one at a time; proved of each step that a streamed response's bytes are `Response.wireChunked` and read back as the head with the parts as its body (`Http.Conn.read_streamed`), that each part is written as its chunk in turn and pulls wait for what was written to be sent (`Http.Conn.pulled_part`, `Http.Conn.flushStream_going`), that a piece is what `Inflow.gather` reads at the connection's position (`Http.Conn.pump_piece`), and that the client's reader of events reads back the events written, in order, each once (`Http.Sse.parse_written`); that the pieces of a whole run make up the strict reader's body is model-checked (`Tests/HttpStream.lean`). `Http.Loopback` drives a front end in tests with no socket. Its strict reader of requests (`Http.Request.read`, `docs/decisions/D49-the-server-reads-requests-by-a-strict-profile.md`) is proved final once it answers (`Http.Request.read_append`), to wait only within its limits and answer within them (`Http.Request.read_more`, `read_done`), to read back what `Request.wire` writes wherever it starts and whatever follows, at its last byte and not before (`read_wire`, `read_wire_extract`), and to refuse a length beside a coding, two lengths, a blank before a colon, obs-fold, a bare CR or LF and a malformed chunk size for every head of those shapes (`read_lengthAndCoding`, `read_twoLengths`, `read_blankInName`, `read_fold`, `read_bareCR`, `read_bareLF`, `read_badChunkSize`); its other refusals, and its verdicts against Go's, Node's and h11's parsers on a corpus, are tested (`oracles/go/requests/requests.py`: stricter or alike on every case). For its operators, each off by default (`ServerConfig.ops`, `docs/decisions/D69-observability.md`): a metrics page in the Prometheus text format (requests by method and status class, latency, connections open and refused, requests in flight, the inbox, the journal's appends and saves), liveness, readiness that answers `200` exactly when the shard has recovered and the server is not stopping or draining (`Http.Ops.answer_ready`, `Server.drain`), request ids taken from a client only when bounded and plain (`Http.Ops.RequestId.accept?_eq_some`), and a JSON access log whose lines are the JSON text of their records (`Http.Ops.Access.parse_line`) and hold no query, header or body; none of it reaches a system, which is trusted and tested: a journal holds the same inputs with all of it on as off | `Lanes/Web/` |

## Next

What is being worked on now, and why: `docs/ROADMAP.md`, "In progress".

## Known limits

- `System.join` leaves the inputs it wires open to the outside until `mapIO` or `filterMapIO`
  hides them, and keeps the outputs it wires in its signature though none is put out;
  `Http.fronted` hides both. A fair run of a join is a fair run of each side
  (`System.Run.Fair.left`, `System.Run.Fair.right`).
- No WebSockets, and no TLS server: TLS is terminated in front, by the load
  balancer or a reverse proxy. The HTTP client speaks HTTP/1.1, plain or over TLS, over IPv4, a
  connection per call, with no proxy (`CONNECT`); a name resolves to its first IPv4 address.
- The client's TLS context, with its trust store, is made for each call (about 3 ms with
  Ubuntu's). Revocation is not checked. OpenSSL fixes reach Lanes with Lean's toolchain. The
  trust store is `SSL_CERT_FILE` when it is set. The C declares the functions of the OpenSSL the
  toolchain links, 4.1.0, and `scripts/tls-declarations.py` checks them against the system's
  headers, 3.0 on Ubuntu 24.04: 4.1's headers are generated from templates by its own build.
- The PostgreSQL client resolves a name to its first IPv4 address at each connect, and takes
  IPv6 addresses but no IPv6 address of a name; it has no Unix sockets, no `PGSERVICE` or
  `~/.postgresql/root.crt`, and does not check a password file's permissions. It has no client certificates,
  no CRL or OCSP check, and its direct TLS is tested against `openssl s_server` only. It has no
  `COPY`, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`, binary formats, named statements or cancellation; the pool does not
  watch idle connections, and `Store.handler` does not use it. A message is decoded through a
  list of bytes, so `message_max` (1 MiB by default) also bounds the memory a reply takes. Its
  live tests run only when `LANES_POSTGRES` or `LANES_POSTGRES_TLS` names a server; CI runs none.
- That a PostgreSQL server behaves like the store model at an isolation level is a premise, tested
  on a few recorded runs, not proved. The model keeps at most `history_max` transactions in its
  serial order while one is open, and a run beyond its bounds is outside it. At read committed,
  `append` is checked for a free key at its answer only.
- Several shards run as several processes joined by TCP (`Lanes.Peers`); there is no router
  between shards in one process any more (D37), so the cores of a machine are used by running a
  process on each. That shards behave as the one system is proved for the semantics, for two
  shards (`Lanes/Runtime/ShardSound.lean`) and for any number (`Lanes/Runtime/ShardsSound.lean`),
  with an actor's shard fixed for the whole run: an actor that moves, or a `Peers.Config.home`
  that is `none`, is outside it. It is not proved for the running program, where it is still
  trusted that the runtimes and the transport implement `System.shards` with links between
  shards no better than `Link.network`.
- A boot actor that stops as it starts does not behave the same on several shards: the shards
  boot one after another, so a message another boot actor sent it may be kept where the one
  system loses it (`Tests/Split.lean`, `fragile`). The theorem assumes it away
  (`System.SteadyBoot`); invariants of actor states proved for every environment are not
  affected.
- The models of external services are not tested against a real service: the adapters for
  them, the S3 client and the AWS integration's SES, run against fakes, and the other recorded runs are written by hand from
  the documentation. Idempotency keys do
  not expire in the model; a real payment service forgets them after 24 hours. Requests other
  than one that makes a thing (retrieve, list, cancel, refund) are not modelled.
- The S3 client sends and receives whole bodies, in memory, within the HTTP client's
  `maxResponseBytes`, a multipart upload's whole body too (`S3.upload` sends it a part at a
  time, one part after another); videos go between the browser and S3 through a `POST` form and
  presigned links. Credentials
  come from the environment, are given, or are read at each call from a source (`SigV4.Source`),
  such as the AWS integration's. It has not
  been run against AWS, MinIO or LocalStack, nor over TLS in a test; the XML reader, scoped to
  S3's answers, is not yet tested against Go's. No conditional write. That S3 refuses a presigned
  part whose `Content-Length` is not the one signed is believed, not checked against AWS; moto
  reads no `POST` policy, so what S3 refuses under one is checked against AWS's example and
  botocore only.
- The AWS integration has not run against AWS: the metadata service, a container's endpoint and
  SES are fakes written from AWS's documentation as remembered. Credentials come from IMDSv2 or a
  container's endpoint only (no profiles, SSO or STS), over IPv4, and are kept in memory, fetched
  again at each start. SES sends simple messages (no attachments, templates or raw MIME), to
  bare addresses, with no webhooks; it takes no idempotency key, so a send whose answer was lost
  may be sent twice if it is sent again.
- CloudFront's signed URLs and cookies (`Aws.CloudFront`) have not run against CloudFront: they
  are compared with botocore's `CloudFrontSigner`, and what CloudFront takes is read from AWS's
  SDKs, not its documentation. The cookies have no `Domain`, so they reach CloudFront only when it
  serves the site's own host. Keys are RSA of 2048 bits or P-256, in a PEM that is not encrypted;
  a policy's addresses are IPv4.
- The cache, wall-clock, shared-cache and throttling models have no adapter and no recorded run
  of a real system. The queue's calls (`Aws.Sqs`) have no handler and have run against moto
  only, which deletes a message with any receipt it was given. The queue takes a delete as done when it is handed over and has no
  five-minute window for FIFO deduplication; the cache's leases are memcached's, which Redis gives
  only through a script; the wall clock's skew is not measured; the throttling model has one caller.
- A job submitted when `maxInFlight` jobs are active is refused, not queued.
- Beside a system, that the answer reaches the requester, and at most once, is not yet carried
  through the join: it is proved of the jobs actor alone.
- An attempt whose deadline passes keeps running in its worker; a pure worker cannot be cut
  off, so the work done at once can exceed `maxInFlight`.
- The scheduler's time is what it was told and what its timers were armed for: after a long time
  without input, or after a start, a job may be late by that much; that it is never early rests
  on the times it is told and on the runtime's timers (`TRUSTED.md`).
- A scheduling when `maxJobs` jobs are held is refused, not queued.
- What `Lanes.Base64`, `Lanes.Ip` and `Lanes.TimeFormat` refuse is stated by theorems only for
  Base64 (`decode` accepts exactly the canonical text); for addresses and dates, that they refuse
  what Go refuses is tested, not proved, on the oracle's generated cases.
- Base64 recurses once per four characters, so a very long input (megabytes) uses stack in
  proportion.
- IPv6 zones (`fe80::1%eth0`) are refused, also in URLs, and a leap second (`23:59:60`) is not a
  time.
- What `Lanes.Url` and `Lanes.MediaType` refuse is tested against Go, not proved. A URL's IP
  literal is kept as an address and printed as RFC 5952 writes it, so `print (parse s)` is `s`
  only up to that; IPvFuture literals are refused. Rate limits have no table of buckets per key
  yet.
- The checker runs about 50,000 states per second on one core (the election model: 164,847
  states in 3.0 to 3.7 s, against 10.8 to 11.2 s before the work of D33), and its tasks do not
  help: Lean counts references to shared objects atomically and never updates them in place,
  so four workers cost two to three times the processor time for no gain in wall time. At
  this rate ten million states take over three minutes and, stored exactly, about 7 GB (0.75 kB
  a state on the election model). The next factor needs states that are flat data (D33).
- A refinement check (`Check.refines`) takes 15 to 30 times as long as a plain check of the same
  system: the monitor keeps a candidate for each order in which the inputs in flight may have
  taken effect (92 for the five requests of the tutorial's shelf), and closing them is quadratic
  in their number. `lake exe lanesCheck` prints the shelf's times (`Tests/MonitorSpeed.lean`).
- Liveness theorems are about fair runs of the semantics. That the runtime's runs are fair is
  not proved, and "eventually" carries no bound.
- A journal is cut only if the application gives codecs for its actors (`Journal.Store.actors`,
  `Http.Saving`); without them it grows without bound and a restart replays all of it. A
  codec's law is an equality, so a state that holds a map holds a `Std.ExtTreeMap`
  (`Codec.extTreeMap`): a `TreeMap` or a `HashMap` has no codec. The codecs are derived
  by `lanes_data` from the declarations of the state and the messages, or written with
  `Codec.struct%` and `Codec.sum%` for a type it does not accept (recursive, with indices). The
  order in which a save replaces the journal's past is proved to lose nothing wherever the
  process dies (`Journal.Disk.Holds.save_crash`), over a model of the two files. That the
  operating system's rename is atomic, that flushed bytes survive the process and that synced ones
  survive a loss of power is trusted. Every flushed write is synced (`fsync`), about 0.2 ms a
  batch on the disk it was measured on.
- A journal is begun at any path that has none, unless the store says otherwise
  (`Journal.Store.create`). An application whose shard makes promises to others, as a Raft
  node does with its vote, has to say so itself, as `raftNode` does.
- A migration needs the old version's system, its step functions and codecs, in the new binary
  for as long as files of that version may exist. `Http.serve` takes no upgrades yet: its
  system is the application's behind the gate, and a migration would have to be lifted through
  the gate. What carries over a migration is what each new actor keeps by its own steps; an
  invariant proved only from boot, or refinement, does not, and a shard migrated twice is
  covered by `Journal.Upgrade.inv_load` only for the first migration.
- A journal's name has to cover everything its replay reads: the version of the step
  functions and every setting they use, timeouts among them, since a timer is due at the
  clock's reading plus the configured delay. Nothing checks that a name does. `raft-kv` puts
  its whole `Config` in the name, so a timeout of a node that has run cannot be changed.
- A save writes the whole kernel, and the shard does nothing else meanwhile. `raft-kv` never
  compacts its log, so a node's snapshot grows with every command it has ever taken.
- Cutting off a write that did not finish, and cutting a journal at a save, replace the
  journal file by a new one, which gets default permissions; `.tmp` files left by a process
  killed in between are not cleaned up.
- A timer does not advance while the process is down, and after a restart it also loses the
  time that had passed since the last journal entry before the process died.
- A step that emits very many outputs is quadratic in their number (`Kernel.performAll`
  appends one at a time): 20,000 outputs from one step take most of a second.
- The runtime releases only an actor whose state is one a start gives it (`Actor.fresh`, which
  an actor declares; the default declares none). An actor that is idle in any other state keeps
  its cell for good, so a session-per-user system still grows with its users. Releasing it means
  its state must live somewhere else, so this waits for the persistence adapter.
- The events a releasing kernel reports are a run of the semantics but for the starts that
  bring released actors back, so a replay through `SysState.run` must skip a start of an actor
  that is up. Declaring `fresh` changes what an old journal replays to: its name must change.
- One shard takes about 1.8 million inputs a second from one sender and about a million from
  four that contend for its inbox, on a four-core machine; its kernel alone does between two
  and three million turns a second. With a journal every batch is one write, so the disk is
  the limit there. A shard with nothing to do sleeps, and waking it costs tens of microseconds.
- That a pending timer fires in time is proved as far as the kernel goes: its agenda holds
  exactly the pending timers, it never tells the shell to sleep past one, and it fires one that
  is due on its next step or, when a message is waiting too, the step after
  (`Kernel.exec_wellFormed`, `Kernel.WellFormed.wait_of_due`, `step_of_due`, `wait_for_ms`).
  That the clock advances and the shell's sleep ends is assumed (see `TRUSTED.md`).
- The kernel's message queue has no bound of its own (see `TRUSTED.md`).
- Work outside a step goes through the jobs actor (`Lanes.Jobs`). On a journal, a job whose
  result was not journalled when the process died is attempted again with its key, so a far
  side that must not act twice has to deduplicate by it.
- Actors step in parallel only with `Runtime.Config.workers` above one, and then only within a
  wave, their steps committed in queue order by one thread; the gate of an HTTP server is one
  actor. A step handed to another thread costs a microsecond or two more, in Lean's reference
  counts of objects threads share, so cheap steps run slower that way
  (`docs/decisions/D64-actors-run-in-parallel.md`).
- Lean never updates in place an object another thread has seen, so each actor the pool steps
  has its state copied once a wave, in its task, and once more by its next step on the shard's
  thread. With `parallel := .on`, a write to one of two busy actors whose states hold a million
  numbers costs about a tenth of a millisecond, where it costs a microsecond on the shard's thread.
  `.auto` keeps such steps on the shard's thread (`docs/decisions/D88-waves-in-place.md`).
- The fake S3 checks signatures with the functions the client signs with, so it agrees with the
  client by construction; that they are S3's is tested against AWS's vectors (`Tests/SigV4.lean`).
- The browser runs no script and follows no redirect, and ignores a cookie's domain, expiry and
  `Secure`.
- Without the `openssl` command the fake provider issues no ID token.
- `lanes lint` is text-level, but for the inventory. `no-io-in-step`, `bounded`, `field-leak`
  and `fn-length` need the elaborator and are not implemented.
- The inventory's "proved" is only as strong as the gates: a gated theorem covers every
  definition its statement names and what those run in their own module, whether or not it
  says all they are for. A test or a check covers what it names in the same way, which makes the
  checker's own plumbing (`Check.Report.ok`, `Inspect`) "checked" because checks use it.
  `lanes_data`, `macro_rules` and `elab_rules` are invisible to it: a test uses the syntax, not
  a constant. `LanesCli/` is listed but not held to the list of definitions without evidence.
- The warm runner machine, its CloudFormation stack and the start and stop jobs have been checked
  with linters and stubs only, not yet run against AWS.
- Templates take text children as string literals (`<p>"text"</p>`), not bare text.
- The gate keeps waiting requests in a list, so each request costs time linear in `maxPending`.
- Behind `Http.serveShard` a response must be put out by an actor of the process that took the
  request. Request ids are each process's own, so a response put out on another shard reaches
  that shard's gate, which may be waiting on the same id for another client. Nothing prevents
  this; `Tests/Fronted.lean` shows the mild case, a `504` at the front that took the request.
- Templates cannot contain inline `<script>` or `<style>` text, and `render` gives those
  elements no children; URL attributes accept only relative, `http`, `https`, `mailto` and `tel`
  URLs. An attribute that holds code or markup (`onclick`, `srcdoc`, `style`) takes its value as
  given, escaped: what it means is the application's.
- The browser model of `Html.lex_render` is the tokenizer's data and double-quoted-attribute
  states: a browser also lowercases names, keeps the first of two attributes of one name, and
  reads the content of `title`, `textarea`, `noscript` and the other raw text elements as text.
- A purpose of `Auth.sign` must have no zero byte, and `form` is the purpose of form tokens.
- Sign-in: the key of the tickets and the states used live in memory, so a restart refuses the
  callbacks of sign-ins begun before it; a full set of states used (`maxUsed`) refuses sign-ins
  begun before the states it dropped; no refresh
  tokens, no UserInfo endpoint, no `.well-known` fetched at run time, no RFC 9207 `iss` on the
  callback; ID tokens of RS256 and ES256 only; `iat`, `auth_time`, `acr` and `at_hash` are not
  checked. With `arrive`, requests of one connection may enter the system out of order.
- The server writes no `Date` header, and answers an unknown method `501`.
- The head of a request, and a chunked body, is read again from its start each time bytes of
  it arrive, so one sent a byte at a time costs time quadratic in its length, within its limit
  and its deadline.
- The connection's own refusals (`400`, `408`, `413`, `431`, `501`) are neither counted in the
  metrics nor logged. The metrics page and the health checks are on the application's port; the
  page is answered only to a loopback peer by default, and the health checks to every peer.
- A response streams to an HTTP/1.0 client in chunks, which it does not read. A body that
  streams is no longer handed on once the client ends its side. That the pieces of a whole run
  make up the body, and the bytes of a whole stream the parts given, is model-checked, not proved.
  A request that streams, its pieces and its pulls pass by `ServerConfig.ops` and `arrive`.
- No adapter: the shop runs only in the checker and the proof.
- No form token: anyone who can reach the server can schedule and cancel.
- After a start the sweep runs at once, and a reminder due while the process was down is late.
- Sessions are signed with a key made at start, so they end with the process, and the members
  are not journalled; neither the example nor its presets has been run against Google or GitHub.
- That no to-do is stored twice is checked, for one and two to-dos, not proved: the proof covers
  the actor, and the rest rests on the table's primary key, a premise of the store model.
- The actor's state is volatile: a crash forgets the to-dos waiting.
- Not run against AWS or a real provider; `videosLive` runs the flow against a bucket the
  environment names. Links handed out before a delete last until they expire. Every page view is
  journalled. No search or mail (its README). No worker that speaks the transcode format but the
  test kit's, and a round under way has no deadline. A journal of before the pipeline (`videos
  2`) is refused, not upgraded.
